overview: The map’s “Rift Valley States” label groups part of Africa’s Great Lakes region in 1783 to 1815. It was no single kingdom: Bunyoro, Buganda, Rwanda, Burundi and neighbouring states had different rulers and histories. The examples below distinguish earlier archaeology, the kingdoms’ expansion, and later records of crafts and daily life.

periods.title: Expanding regional powers
periods.summary: Buganda gained territory and influence during the eighteenth century; Rwanda emerged as a major power farther south.

periods.title: Several kingdoms continue
periods.summary: Buganda’s prominence and Bunyoro’s changing fortunes continued into the nineteenth century. This map interval is not a common reign or dynasty.

items.text: Different landscapes supported different combinations of work. In the histories of Bunyoro and Buganda, cattle, grain and banana farming, fishing, hunting and metalworking all mattered. Political power grew from these local resources and relationships, rather than requiring a coastal trading empire to create it.

Buganda expanded partly by placing royal appointees in newly acquired territory. Such officials could challenge older hereditary chiefs. Building a larger kingdom therefore changed who collected resources and exercised authority in people’s home communities, as well as moving a line on a map.

Long before the mapped period, Ntusi in western Uganda combined sorghum cultivation with cattle grazing, around 1000 to 1400. Cattle bones, charred grain and broken pots recover ordinary meals and work from a settlement whose history cannot be reduced to a list of kings.

Ntusi also had two enormous rubbish mounds, roughly five metres high. Their accumulated household waste points to organized disposal. To an archaeologist, an ancient rubbish heap can be a wonderfully informative archive; somebody’s broken pot has finally found a new job.

Karagwe, in what is now northwestern Tanzania, preserved a royal treasury of iron standards, weapons, pillar anvils and animal sculptures. Some were traditionally attributed to the early nineteenth-century king Ndagara, remembered as a skilled smith. The attribution connects craftsmanship with royal authority, although it does not establish who forged every surviving object.

Two iron cattle figures from that Karagwe tradition have enormous curving horns. Curators interpret them as powerful leaders of the royal herds, associated with fertility and community welfare. Cattle could therefore represent nourishment, wealth and sacred responsibility in the same carefully worked sculpture.

A later, twentieth-century Baganda milk container shows how carefully household equipment could be designed. Its wooden body has a broad, stable base and a narrow neck protected by a woven cover. Keeping flies out of the milk was a practical design problem, not a glamorous royal one.

Twentieth-century accounts discussed by the museum describe women cleaning and fumigating milk containers while men milked cattle. Pots rested on raised platforms inside homes. These are dated examples of shared household responsibilities in pastoral communities, not a rule that every Great Lakes family followed.

sections.title: Travelling and trading: a later eyewitness

items.text: In 1862, after this map window, Speke travelled toward Bunyoro in vessels made from five planks tied together and sealed with cloth. Paddlers, passengers, animals and provisions shared the boats. Skilled construction made rivers useful roads through the region.

On that journey, he encountered Banyoro traders in dugout canoes returning from Busoga with cloth, dried fish, plantains and beer. This was trade between African communities across political boundaries. The episode also describes an attack on their cargo, showing how authority and violence could interrupt everyday exchange.

sections.title: Reading, translation and a small book

items.text: A later written-language witness comes from the Luganda Bible produced in sections from 1890 to 1896. Its catalogue-transcribed title begins Ekitabo ekitukuvu ekya Katonda, meaning “The Holy Book of God.” This is Luganda in the Latin alphabet, well after 1815; it is not a claim that these printed words circulated during the map’s earlier period.

Translation was collaborative. Baganda Christians worked alongside missionaries, and Henry Wright Dutamaguzi, known as Duta, helped translate major portions. The institutional account records seventeen men and fourteen women working on translations in 1891. Local readers and translators helped shape this new written religious literature.

The chunky volume became known as the Biscuit Tin Bible. Its small dimensions came from sections designed to fit into people’s cloth bags, according to the library’s account, rather than being specially invented for a biscuit tin. Portability mattered to readers, even before pocket-sized electronic books.

ending.text: The regional kingdoms did not disappear together in 1815. Their nineteenth-century histories continued along different paths, including further expansion and contraction. The end of this imported label marks a change in map coverage, not the end of Great Lakes societies.
